episodes.title: The Astronaut Whose Helmet Filled With Water
episodes.description: July 2013, outside the International Space Station: 44 minutes into a spacewalk, cold water started leaking into astronaut Luca Parmitano's helmet. Then the sun set. This is how he got back without being able to see, guided only by his safety cable.
episodes.style_tail: , cold blue and white palette with warm sun glints, epic movie still

character.prompt: an adult human figure with realistic proportions rendered as a smooth featureless matte white mannequin with a blank egg-shaped head and no facial features, wearing a bulky plain white spacesuit with a clear bubble helmet, floating outside a space station above Earth, full body, three-quarter view

shots.say: Water was crawling over his eyes,
shots.edit: Extreme close-up of the helmet: the clear helmet is half filled with water, the waterline cuts across the blank egg-shaped head, bubbles and droplets inside, harsh sunlight, black space and a sliver of Earth behind.

shots.say: and he was outside the space station.
shots.edit: Extreme wide shot: the same astronaut is tiny, clinging to the long metal truss of the space station, huge golden solar panels, the curved blue Earth far below, black space.

shots.say: {July 2013.|July, twenty thirteen.} Astronaut Luca Parmitano,
shots.edit: Low-angle medium shot: the astronaut grips a handrail on the outside of the space station, Earth curving behind, bright sunlight.

shots.say: on a routine spacewalk.
shots.edit: Wide shot: two identical faceless astronauts in the same white spacesuits work on the exterior of the space station with tethered tools, golden solar panels, Earth below.

shots.say: {44|Forty-four} minutes in, he felt water on the back of his head.
shots.edit: Close-up from behind the helmet: glistening beads of water collect at the back of the helmet around the blank head, soft blue light.

shots.say: Everyone assumed his drink bag was leaking.
shots.prompt: a dim mission control room with rows of glowing monitors, smooth featureless matte white mannequin figures with blank egg-shaped heads wearing headsets seen from behind, a large wall screen showing a live view of an astronaut above Earth

shots.say: It wasn't.
shots.prompt: macro shot of a perfect floating sphere of water in zero gravity against darkness, tiny air bubbles inside it, light refracting through it

shots.say: The water was cold, and it tasted like metal.
It was coming from the suit's own cooling system.
shots.prompt: x-ray cutaway visualization of a white spacesuit backpack life support system, glowing blue coolant tubes, a small fan pump and water separator leaking water from a clogged part, dark background

shots.say: It covered his eyes. His ears. His nose.
Mission Control called the spacewalk off.
Then the sun went down.
shots.edit: Orbital sunset: the astronaut floats weightless in the foreground as a dark silhouette, a thin glowing band of orange and deep blue on Earth's horizon behind him, a solar panel silhouette.

shots.say: Total darkness.
shots.edit: Night in orbit, almost total darkness: only the astronaut's small headlamp beam lights a metal handrail on the station, everything else is black.

shots.say: He couldn't even see the handrails in front of him.
His radio was drowning too.
He was alone.
shots.edit: Extreme wide shot: the astronaut is a tiny lone figure floating in black space high above the dark night side of Earth, city lights far below.

shots.say: So he followed the only thing he could feel:
shots.edit: Close-up of the astronaut's white glove gripping a thin steel safety tether cable in darkness, a headlamp glint on the metal.

shots.say: his safety cable, pulling him back.
shots.edit: Wide shot at night outside the space station: a thin tether cable runs along the hull toward a small glowing open airlock hatch, the astronaut pulls himself along it hand over hand.

shots.say: His last resort? Open a valve by his ear
shots.edit: Close-up of the side of the helmet: the astronaut's gloved fingers reach for a small metal valve on the side of the helmet, dramatic rim light, black space.

shots.say: and dump the water into space.
shots.edit: A burst of water vapor flashes into glittering ice crystals as it vents from the side of the astronaut's helmet into black space, sunlight catching the crystals.

shots.say: He made it to the airlock with his eyes closed.
They found about {1.5 liters|one and a half liters} of water in his helmet.
shots.prompt: inside a space station module, a white spacesuit helmet resting on a panel with a large wobbling ball of water floating out of it, smooth featureless matte white mannequin figures with blank egg-shaped heads as crew members standing around it, cool interior light

shots.say: And the worst part?
shots.edit: The same spacesuit, empty, hanging in a dim locker on the space station, lit by a single cold light, ominous.

shots.say: The same suit had leaked a week earlier.
No one dug deeper.
shots.prompt: smooth featureless matte white mannequin figures with blank egg-shaped heads as engineers walking away from an empty white spacesuit standing on a stand in a dim hangar, a single spotlight

shots.say: Until the water was crawling over his eyes...

episodes.title: The Man Lightning Struck Seven Times
episodes.description: Park ranger Roy Sullivan was struck by lightning seven times between 1942 and 1977, a Guinness World Record. Toenail, eyebrows, shoulder, hair (three times)... and after the seventh, he still had to fight a bear for his fish.
episodes.style_tail: , stormy teal and electric white palette, 1970s Appalachian setting, epic movie still

character.prompt: an adult human figure with realistic proportions rendered as a smooth featureless matte white mannequin with a blank egg-shaped head and no facial features, dressed as a 1970s park ranger in a khaki uniform shirt, khaki trousers, brown boots and a flat-brimmed campaign hat, standing on a forest trail, full body, three-quarter view

shots.say: Lightning hits him right on the top of the head.
shots.edit: He stands knee deep in a mountain stream at night holding a fishing rod while a blinding white lightning bolt strikes the top of his hat from a black storm sky, sparks and crackling electricity, rain.

shots.say: His hair catches fire.
shots.edit: Close-up from behind and slightly above: the top of his campaign hat is scorched and smoking with small flames and glowing embers rising into the rain, dark storm.

shots.say: And this... is the seventh time.
shots.prompt: seven jagged lightning bolts striking at once across a black storm sky over forested Appalachian mountains, epic extreme wide shot

shots.say: Roy Sullivan was a park ranger
shots.edit: Seen from behind, he stands on a rocky mountain overlook, layers of blue ridge mountains in haze, golden hour.

shots.say: in Shenandoah National Park.
shots.prompt: aerial view of the Blue Ridge Mountains with a winding scenic road through autumn forest, mist in the valleys, golden light

shots.say: Strike one, {1942.|nineteen forty-two.}
shots.prompt: a wooden fire lookout tower on a mountain peak engulfed in flames during a thunderstorm at night, lightning in the sky

shots.say: He runs from a burning fire tower, and a bolt takes his big toenail.
shots.edit: He sprints away from a burning wooden fire lookout tower as a lightning bolt hits the ground right at his feet, sparks flying, rain, dynamic motion.

shots.say: {1969:|Nineteen sixty-nine:} lightning comes through his truck window
shots.prompt: a vintage 1960s pickup truck on a mountain road at night, a lightning bolt striking through the open driver window, the cab interior lit blue-white

shots.say: and burns off his eyebrows.
{1970:|Nineteen seventy:} his own front yard. It sears his shoulder.
shots.edit: In the front yard of a small rural house at dusk, a lightning arc jumps from a power transformer on a wooden pole to his shoulder, sparks.

shots.say: {1972:|Nineteen seventy-two:} inside a ranger station. His hair catches fire.
shots.edit: Inside a rustic wooden ranger station during a storm, a halo of electric sparks crackles around his hat, the window flashing white.

shots.say: After that, he kept a can of water in his truck.
shots.prompt: a dented metal water can on the bench seat of a vintage pickup truck, rain streaking the windshield, moody light

shots.say: {1973:|Nineteen seventy-three:} hair on fire. Again.
{1976:|Nineteen seventy-six:} he swears a cloud is following him.
shots.edit: Tiny on a forest trail, he looks up at a huge dark swirling storm cloud hanging low over the trees, ominous.

shots.say: He runs.
shots.edit: He runs down a muddy forest trail away from the storm, rain, dynamic low angle.

shots.say: It gets him anyway.
shots.edit: A lightning bolt strikes him as he runs on the forest trail, blinding flash, sparks, rain.

shots.say: Guinness puts the odds of being struck even once at about {1 in 10,000.|one in ten thousand.}
shots.prompt: top-down view of thousands of tiny glowing featureless mannequin figures standing in a dark field at night, one single figure lit by a thin lightning bolt from above

shots.say: People started avoiding him.
shots.edit: He stands alone under a dark sky while a group of identical faceless mannequin coworkers in ranger uniforms walk away from him.

shots.say: In one storm, his own chief ranger walked away: "I'll see you later."
And that day in {1977?|nineteen seventy-seven?}
shots.prompt: a mountain stream right after a storm, steam rising off the rocks, a fishing rod lying on the bank, golden light breaking through clouds

shots.say: After the seventh strike, a bear tried to steal his trout.
shots.edit: By a mountain stream after rain, a black bear wades in and reaches for a trout hanging on his fishing line while he stands behind it.

shots.say: He hit it with a branch.
shots.edit: He swings a tree branch at a black bear beside the stream, splashing water, dramatic action.

shots.say: So what do you do after six lightning strikes?
You go fishing.

episodes.title: What If You Opened a Plane Door at 35,000 Feet?
episodes.description: Could a passenger really open an airliner door mid-flight? At cruise, cabin pressure jams the plug door shut with more than 20,000 pounds of force. But in 2023 one passenger did open an exit door, at 700 feet. Here's the physics.
episodes.style_tail: , warm sunset amber and deep blue palette, generic modern airliner with plain white livery, epic movie still

shots.say: You grab the emergency exit handle at {35,000 feet,|thirty-five thousand feet,} and pull.
shots.prompt: close-up: a smooth featureless white mannequin hand firmly gripping the red emergency exit door handle inside an airliner cabin, the small door window beside it shows clouds far below at sunset, tense dramatic light

shots.say: Nothing happens.
shots.prompt: an airliner emergency exit door seen from inside, sealed tight in its frame, a smooth white mannequin hand on the half-raised red handle, warm cabin light, the wing visible through the small window

shots.say: It's not the lock. It's the air.
shots.prompt: cutaway visualization of an airliner fuselage in flight above clouds, glowing blue arrows of air pressure pushing outward on the cabin walls and doors from inside, 3D technical render

shots.say: At cruising altitude, the cabin air pushes
shots.prompt: a modern airliner cruising high above a sea of clouds at sunset, seen from the side, contrails

shots.say: about {8.5 pounds|eight and a half pounds} harder on every square inch
shots.prompt: 3D visualization: an airliner door seen from inside, thousands of tiny glowing blue air particles packed densely on the cabin side pushing against it, only a few sparse particles outside, dark background

shots.say: than the air outside.
And the door is a plug.
shots.prompt: 3D technical cutaway of an airliner plug door that is larger than its frame, wedged into the opening from the inside like a drain stopper, glowing outline, dark background

shots.say: It has to move inward before it can open.
So you're not pulling a handle.
You're pulling against more than {20,000 pounds.|twenty thousand pounds.}
shots.prompt: surreal visualization of a gigantic stack of black steel weight plates pressing against the outside of an airliner door in the sky, clouds below, cinematic

shots.say: About ten tons.
But it has been opened.
shots.prompt: an airliner emergency exit door forced partly open in flight, a blinding strip of daylight and the ground visible through the gap, wind

shots.say: {May 2023.|May, twenty twenty-three.}
shots.prompt: an airliner on final approach descending over a city at midday, landing gear down, haze

shots.say: An Asiana jet, {700 feet|seven hundred feet} above Daegu.
shots.prompt: view through an airliner window during low final approach: rooftops, roads and the start of a runway close below, bright daylight

shots.say: A passenger forces the exit door partly open.
shots.prompt: inside an airliner cabin, an emergency exit door in the left cabin wall pushed partly open with a blinding gap of daylight sky, napkins and papers blowing through the air, smooth featureless matte white mannequin figures with blank egg-shaped heads as passengers leaning away from the door in their seats

shots.say: Wind blasts through the cabin.
Twelve people go to the hospital.
shots.prompt: flashing red and blue emergency lights reflecting on wet tarmac beside a parked airliner at dusk, the emergency vehicles out of focus far in the background

shots.say: The plane lands safely.
Near the ground, the pressure difference almost vanishes.
And up high? In {2024,|twenty twenty-four,} a door plug blew out of an Alaska Airlines jet
shots.prompt: a gaping rectangular hole torn in the side of an airliner fuselage in flight, cabin lights visible inside, clouds below, dramatic

shots.say: at almost {15,000 feet.|fifteen thousand feet.}
shots.prompt: view from inside an airliner cabin toward a large rectangular hole torn in the cabin wall next to a row of empty seats, bright sky and clouds through the hole, torn insulation around the edges, oxygen masks dangling

shots.say: Headrests, a tray table, wall panels, gone.
shots.prompt: a folding tray table and two small headrest cushions tumbling through open sky with clouds far below, motion blur, an airliner flying away in the distance

shots.say: Everyone survived.
shots.prompt: smooth featureless matte white mannequin figures with blank egg-shaped heads as airline passengers sitting calmly in their seats wearing small yellow plastic oxygen mask cups on clear tubes, cabin in daylight

shots.say: At {35,000 feet,|thirty-five thousand feet,} after a sudden decompression,
shots.prompt: small yellow plastic oxygen mask cups on clear tubes dropping from open ceiling panels above rows of airliner seats, swinging, a light fog in the cabin air

shots.say: you'd have maybe {15 to 30 seconds|fifteen to thirty seconds} of useful consciousness.
shots.prompt: a blurry tunnel-vision view of an airliner cabin aisle with darkening edges, one yellow oxygen mask dangling in sharp focus

shots.say: That's why the masks drop.
So. You're in the exit row, at {35,000 feet...|thirty-five thousand feet...}

episodes.title: Could You Really Outrun a Tsunami?
episodes.description: A tsunami crosses the deep ocean as fast as a jet and still hits the beach at the speed of a car. The fastest human ever measured hit 27.8 mph. So can you outrun one? In 2004 a 10-year-old girl showed the real answer.
episodes.style_tail: , tropical turquoise and ominous grey palette, epic movie still

shots.say: The sea just pulled back.

shots.say: Wet sand where the waves used to be.
shots.prompt: close-up of a fish lying on wet sand and pebbles exposed to the open air where the sea used to be, small tide pools and coral, a small boat lying on its side on the sand behind, overcast sky

shots.say: People walk out to look.

shots.say: Don't.

shots.say: Near shore it slows down,

shots.say: to about {20 or 30.|twenty or thirty.}

shots.say: The speed of a car.
The fastest human ever measured, Usain Bolt,
shots.prompt: a smooth featureless white mannequin sprinter exploding out of the starting blocks on a running track at night under stadium floodlights, backlit

shots.say: hit {27.8.|twenty-seven point eight.}
For a moment. On a perfect track.
shots.prompt: an empty red running track with white lane lines under stadium floodlights at night, low angle, wet surface reflections

shots.say: You're on soft sand. In flip-flops.
shots.prompt: close-up of the feet of a smooth white mannequin figure in flip-flops sinking into soft sand while running, sand flying, low angle

shots.say: And a tsunami isn't one wave.

shots.say: The first may not be the biggest, and the danger can last for hours.

shots.say: So no, you can't outrun it.
shots.prompt: a lone smooth featureless white mannequin figure sprinting across the sand toward the camera, a gigantic breaking wave towering right behind it, spray filling the air

shots.say: But in {2004,|two thousand four,} a ten-year-old girl on a beach in Thailand didn't try to.

shots.say: Tilly Smith saw the water frothing, like beer,
shots.prompt: close-up of strange bubbling white froth fizzing on the sea surface at the shoreline, like beer foam, bright sunlight

shots.say: and remembered a geography lesson from two weeks earlier.
shots.prompt: a school classroom with a projector screen showing an old black and white film of an ocean wave, smooth featureless matte white mannequin figures with blank egg-shaped heads as children seen from behind, warm light

shots.say: She warned her parents.

episodes.title: The Astronauts Who Fixed Their Air With Duct Tape
episodes.description: April 1970: an oxygen tank explodes on the way to the Moon, and Apollo 13's crew retreats into a lunar module built for two people for two days. Then the carbon dioxide starts building up, and the spare filters are the wrong shape.
episodes.style_tail: , cold blue cabin light and warm amber warning lights, 1970s NASA hardware, epic movie still

character.prompt: an adult human figure with realistic proportions rendered as a smooth featureless matte white mannequin with a blank egg-shaped head and no facial features, wearing a bulky plain white 1970s spacesuit without a helmet, inside a cramped dim spacecraft cabin lit by small panel lights, full body, three-quarter view

shots.say: The air was slowly poisoning them,
shots.edit: Three identical faceless mannequin astronauts in the same white suits huddle in the cramped, frosty cabin of a lunar module, an amber warning light glowing on the panel beside them.

shots.say: and they were more than {200,000 miles|two hundred thousand miles} from home.
shots.prompt: a tiny Apollo-era spacecraft with a spidery lunar module attached, drifting in black space, the small blue Earth far behind it

shots.say: {April 1970.|April, nineteen seventy.} Apollo 13 is on its way to the Moon,

episodes.title: Could Quicksand Really Swallow You Whole?
episodes.description: Movies say quicksand pulls you under until you vanish. In 2005 physicists rebuilt quicksand in the lab to find out. It can't swallow you, but it can still trap you, and the real danger is something else.

character.prompt: an adult human figure with realistic proportions rendered as a smooth featureless matte white mannequin with a blank egg-shaped head and no facial features, dressed as a hiker in a grey t-shirt, khaki shorts and hiking boots with a small backpack, standing on a wet tidal sand flat near a river delta, full body, three-quarter view

shots.say: In 2005, Daniel Bonn's team rebuilt quicksand in the lab,

shots.prompt: a vast white salt lake under a pale sky with wet sandy shores and distant brown hills, wide shot

shots.say: fine sand, clay and salt water.
shots.prompt: macro shot of wet grains of fine sand and grey clay glistening with salt water

shots.say: Then they dropped in beads as dense as a human body.
shots.prompt: small metal beads dropping into a glass container of wet grey sand in a laboratory, splash of sand, macro

shots.say: The beads sank, but never more than halfway.
shots.prompt: cross-section 3D visualization of a sphere half sunk in sand and stuck, the top half above the surface, glowing outline

shots.say: Because quicksand is denser than you are.
You'd stop around your waist.
shots.edit: The hiker is stuck in the quicksand up to the waist, no longer sinking, hands resting on the surface.

shots.say: So it can't pull you under.
But getting out is the real trap.
shots.edit: Close-up of the hiker's leg and boot buried in thick wet sand, the sand gripping around the knee.

shots.say: Pulling one foot out takes about the force needed to lift a medium-sized car.
shots.prompt: surreal visualization of a small car hanging from a single rope that disappears into wet sand, dramatic light

shots.say: Yank too hard, Bonn warned, and you could pull a person apart.
shots.edit: Two identical faceless mannequin hikers pull the stuck hiker's arms from the firm sand at the edge, straining.

shots.say: The trick is to wiggle your legs slowly,
so water seeps in around them, and the sand lets go.
shots.prompt: macro shot of seawater seeping into a gap in wet sand around a buried boot, glistening

shots.say: So what's actually dangerous?
Quicksand often forms near the sea and big river deltas.
shots.prompt: aerial view of a wide river delta meeting the sea, shining wet sand flats and channels, overcast

shots.say: Get stuck out there, and the tide comes in.
shots.edit: Wide shot: the hiker is stuck to the waist far out on the sand flat while a line of incoming sea water creeps toward them.

shots.say: Quicksand won't swallow you. The ocean might.
shots.prompt: incoming tide water flooding across a shining wet sand flat, low angle, grey sky

shots.say: So remember that, the next time you step onto wet sand.

Humans are less dense than quicksand and sink roughly to the waist
Pulling a foot out takes about the force to lift a medium-size car; pulling hard could pull you into two pieces; wiggle slowly to let water in
Quicksand forms near river deltas / the sea; the real danger is getting stuck when high tide comes up

episodes.title: What If You Fell Into a Black Hole?
episodes.description: Which black hole you fall into changes everything. A NASA supercomputer simulation shows what a plunge into a supermassive black hole would look like, and what an observer far away would see instead.

character.prompt: an adult human figure with realistic proportions rendered as a smooth featureless matte white mannequin with a blank egg-shaped head and no facial features, wearing a sleek modern white spacesuit with a clear helmet, floating in deep space with a faint glowing ring of light in the distance, full body, three-quarter view

shots.say: Which one you fall into changes everything.

shots.say: A small one, left behind when a giant star explodes,
shots.prompt: a massive star exploding in a brilliant supernova in deep space, shock waves of glowing gas

shots.say: has a tiny edge and brutal tidal forces.

shots.prompt: 3D visualization of a long thin stretched streak of glowing matter spiraling into a small black hole, motion blur

shots.say: like the one at our galaxy's center, {4.3 million|four point three million} times the Sun's mass.

shots.say: Its edge, the event horizon, is about {16 million miles|sixteen million miles} across.

episodes.title: What If You Lay Flat When Lightning Strikes?
episodes.description: Caught outside in a thunderstorm, lots of people drop flat on the ground to make themselves small. The National Weather Service says that's a myth, and so are a few other things you've probably heard.
episodes.style_tail: , stormy teal and electric white palette, epic movie still

character.prompt: an adult human figure with realistic proportions rendered as a smooth featureless matte white mannequin with a blank egg-shaped head and no facial features, dressed as a hiker in a red rain jacket, dark trousers and hiking boots, standing in an open grassy field under a dark thunderstorm sky, full body, three-quarter view

shots.say: Lightning's cracking all around you, so you drop flat on the ground.
shots.edit: He lies face down flat in the wet grass of the open field while jagged lightning bolts strike the hills around him under a black sky, rain.

shots.say: It feels safer. Lower. Smaller.
The National Weather Service calls that a myth.
shots.prompt: a dark thunderstorm sky with a single bright lightning bolt over an empty open field, wide shot

shots.say: Lying flat raises your chance of getting hit by deadly ground current.
shots.prompt: 3D visualization of a lightning strike hitting a field with glowing branching currents spreading out across the ground in every direction

shots.say: What about crouching?
shots.edit: He crouches low in the open field with his hands over his head as rain pours down and lightning flashes on the horizon.

shots.say: The Weather Service says crouching doesn't make you safer either.
Hiding under a tree?
shots.edit: He stands under a lone tall tree in the middle of the field, sheltering from the pouring rain.

shots.say: That's the second leading cause of lightning casualties.
shots.prompt: a lightning bolt striking a lone tall tree in an open field, sparks and bark flying, rain

shots.say: And if the storm still looks far away?
shots.prompt: a sunny blue sky over a field with a dark thunderstorm far away on the horizon

shots.say: Lightning can strike more than {10 miles|ten miles} from a storm.
shots.prompt: a thin bolt of lightning shooting out of a distant storm cloud and striking far away under a mostly clear sky

shots.say: They're called bolts from the blue.
Lightning never strikes the same place twice? Also wrong.
shots.prompt: a tall skyscraper with an antenna spire at night, lightning striking the spire, dark city below

shots.say: The Empire State Building gets hit about {23 times|twenty-three times} a year.
So what actually works?
shots.prompt: a sturdy brick house with warm lit windows at the edge of a stormy field, rain

shots.say: Get inside a real building, or a hard-top car with the windows up.
shots.edit: He runs across the wet field toward a parked hard-top car, rain pouring, lightning in the distance.

shots.say: No place outside is safe.
Then wait {30 minutes|thirty minutes} after the last thunder.
shots.edit: He sits inside the car looking out through the rain-streaked windshield at the storm moving away over the field.

shots.say: Because next time lightning's cracking all around you, don't just drop flat on the ground.

facts.claim: Myth: lie flat; fact: it increases the chance of being affected by deadly ground current
Crouching doesn't make you safer outdoors; under a tree is the second leading cause of lightning casualties
Lightning can strike more than 10 miles from a storm ('bolts from the blue' 10-15 miles)
Lightning often strikes the same place; Empire State Building about 23 times a year
Safe shelters: buildings and hard-top vehicles with windows up; never lie flat; no place outside is safe; wait 30 minutes after the last thunder
